"Al-hafirah" is a term the Arabs apply to the first state to which one returns from its end. It is said: "So-and-so returned to al-hafirah" when he reverted to a state of the states. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Returned to al-hafirah over a bald head and gray hair? God forbid from folly and shame!"

The meaning is: "Shall we indeed be returned?" to life after departing from it through death. Mujahid and al-Khalil said: "al-hafirah" is the earth, an active participle (fa'ilah) in the sense of a passive (maf'ulah). It was said: this has the meaning of "al-hafirah." It was also said: it is the foul, changed earth with the bodies of its dead, from their saying: "his teeth were eroded" when they were consumed and their smell changed.

"Al-nakhirah": that which resonates with wind, hollow. From this is the saying of the poet: [p. 529]

It is also related as "tasfarru" (whistles). Most people hold to what we have mentioned. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "al-nakhirah" is that which has not yet been hollowed out, and "al-nakhirah" is that which has decayed.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

"Nakāl" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Some people said: "al-ākhira" refers to His saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than Me﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 38], and "al-ūlā" refers to His saying: ﴿I am your most exalted lord﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 24]. It is reported that he remained forty years after his saying: ﴿I am your most exalted lord﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 24]. It was also said that this period was between the two utterances. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "al-ūlā" is His saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than Me﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 38], and "al-ākhira" is His saying: ﴿I am your most exalted lord﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 24]. Abū Ruzayn said: "al-ūlā" is his disbelief and disobedience, and "al-ākhira" is His saying: ﴿I am your most exalted lord﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 24]. Ibn Zayd said: "al-ūlā" is the worldly life, and "al-ākhira" is the Hereafter, meaning Allah the Exalted seized him with the punishment of Hell and with drowning in this world. Mujāhid said: it is an expression for the first and last of his sins and disbelief, meaning He made an example of him in all of them.

"Nakāl" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and its governing verb, according to Sībawayh's view, is "akhadha" (seized), since it carries that meaning. According to Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mubarrad's view, it is a verb implied from the word "nakāl" itself, as if he had said: "nakkalahu nakāl" (He made an example of him, an exemplary punishment).

Then the Exalted stopped at the place of the lesson with the condition of Pharaoh and his punishment. The statement contains a warning to the disbelievers addressed by the message of Muḥammad (ﷺ). Then He addressed them in a speech from Him, the Exalted, to the whole world, and the intended audience is the disbelievers. It is possible that the meaning is: say to them, O Muḥammad: ﴿Are you more difficult to create﴾, and the verse continues. In this verse there is evidence that the resurrection of bodies from graves is not beyond the power of Allah the Exalted. "Sumk" is the height between the lower surface of the sky, which is near us, and its upper surface, which is adjacent to what is above it. His saying, the Exalted: "fa-sawwāhā" may mean: He created it smooth and level, with no elevation or depression in it. It may also be an expression for perfecting its creation, without intending the meaning of making its surface smooth. And Allah the Exalted knows best how it is.

"Aghṭasha" means: he made dark, and "al-aghṭash" means the blind. From it is the saying of the poet:

I slaughtered for them my weakened she-camel, and their night was pitch-dark and gloomy.

He attributed the night and the forenoon to it (the sky) in terms of them being apparent from it and in it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And after that He spread the earth﴾ indicates that Allah the Exalted created the earth but did not spread it, then He turned to the sky while it was smoke, created it and built it, then after that He spread the earth. What we have said is the one upon which all the verses of the Qur'an are ordered. He attributed the water and pasture to the earth in terms of them appearing from it and within it. "Daḥw al-arḍ" is its spreading out, and from it is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt:

A dwelling He spread out, then He settled us in it, and He established the other, which is more glorious.

The majority read "wal-arḍa" in the accusative, while al-Ḥasan and ʿĪsā read "wal-arḍu" in the nominative. The majority read "wal-jibāla arsāhā" in the accusative, while al-Ḥasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read "wal-jibālu" in the nominative. "Arsāhā" means: He established them firmly. He gathered these blessings: when they are contemplated, they are a provision for people and for "al-anʿām" (livestock), by which they enjoy themselves. The majority read "matāʿan" in the accusative, while Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "matāʿun" in the nominative.
